title: FAQ
text:
Why is PHES-EF needed?

Public health environmental surveillance has evolved, especially during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, with wastewater surveillance being a prominent example. As surveillance methods diversify and expand, there is a need to evaluate these systems to improve the evidence of wastewater surveillance effectiveness, return-on-investment, accountability, transparency, sustainability and trust.
There is also a need for such an evaluation framework as the recent adoption of wastewater-based monitoring has resulted in a lack of standard analytic techniques, with preferred methods for reporting testing data still remaining unclear (1). PHES-EF aims to address this issue as well, as the framework is intended to be adopted by researchers to determine surveillance system performance and create analogous results for comparison within the field.



What is a Delphi consensus study?

The Delphi method is an iterative multi-round approach that uses a series of sequential surveys, interspersed by controlled feedback, to elicit consensus among a group of individuals while maintaining anonymity (2,3). An electronic Delphi (e-Delphi) method will be used to overcome geographic barriers and allow us to engage panellists internationally across various time zones. Delphi surveys relating to health sciences have typically been conducted over a period of 2-3 rounds (4–6). Therefore, a two-round e-Delphi survey paired with a subsequent consensus meeting will be conducted to balance feasibility with rigour. Each round will be open for about five weeks to allow panellists sufficient time to participate in the survey, while balancing study timeline constraints (7). Each round takes about an hour to complete. The consensus meeting will be held in a hybrid or virtual format.



When will the study take place?

Registration for e-Delphi panellists opens in January 2027. Round 1 runs in March 2027, Round 2 closes in May 2027, and the consensus meeting is planned for September or October 2027. See the e-Delphi study timeline for details.



Who is eligible to participate in the study?

The eligibility criteria for e-Delphi survey panellists can be found on the e-Delphi study page.

PHES-EF is in its second step: generating the candidate evaluation items that panellists will rate in the e-Delphi survey. Two scoping reviews have mapped how surveillance systems are evaluated across public health, animal health, One Health and wastewater surveillance. The terms they identified have been reconciled into a draft framework, which the executive group is reviewing before the survey opens in 2027. This page summarizes that work and shows what panellists will see.

  4OrganizeTerms arranged into themes, domains and attributes, then reviewed by the executive group.

Evidence from the scoping reviews

DescriptionAn explanation of the term that builds on the definition.

Timeliness measures how much time passes as a health event moves through the surveillance system toward public health action. (Azofeifa 2018; CDC 1988) How much timeliness a system needs depends on the health event: rapid reporting is critical for acute, highly transmissible diseases, whereas less urgent conditions allow slower reporting. (Declich 1994; CDC 2001) It is influenced by how the surveillance system is designed, the resources available, and the volume and complexity of the data. (Groseclose & Buckeridge 2017; Declich 1994; Sosin 2003) Delays in laboratory results or data flow can hinder a timely response, particularly in resource-limited settings. (Innes 2022; Sahal 2009) Poor timeliness can also reduce the usefulness of the data and the acceptability of the surveillance system. (Sahal 2009; ECDC 2014; Buehler 2004)



BackgroundThe historical development, theoretical foundations and evidence base that establish the concept’s importance in surveillance system evaluation.

Timeliness has been part of surveillance evaluation since the earliest public health guidelines, which described it as “the speed or delay between steps in a surveillance system” and set the interval between a health event and its reporting, the identification of trends or outbreaks, and the implementation of control measures. (CDC 1988; Thacker 1988) The updated guidelines kept this framing, noting that “the time interval linking any two of these steps can be examined”, and judged the attribute by the availability of information for control. (CDC 2001) Later guidance anchored the interval as early as exposure to the agent and carried it through to the start of control measures. (Buehler 2004; Health Canada 2004; WHO 2006) Standardized terminology for animal health surveillance then settled on a common formulation: “the time between any two defined steps in a surveillance system”. (Hoinville 2013; Drewe 2015)
In public health surveillance, timeliness is treated as a core attribute, measured as the interval between defined steps and interpreted according to the purpose the system serves. (Groseclose 2010; Groseclose & Buckeridge 2017; Sosin 2003) Animal health frameworks use the same definition, applying it through both quantitative and semi-quantitative assessment methods. (Hoinville 2013; Muellner 2018; Peyre 2019) One Health evaluations adopt the same formulation while noting practical constraints, notably the laboratory delays that lengthen the measured interval. (Innes 2022; Peyre 2022) Wastewater-based surveillance recasts it as “the ability of the WS to deliver timely results and to provide an early warning signal compared to other surveillance systems”, gauged by the lead time between environmental and clinical indicators. (Amato 2023) The underlying definition is consistent across disciplines; differences lie mainly in which steps each setting measures, though European public health guidance also labels the concept reactivity. (Groseclose & Buckeridge 2017; Peyre 2019; ECDC 2014)



Evaluation methods (10)The methods or tools used to quantify an attribute.


Interval measurement between defined steps: measuring the time elapsing between any two defined steps in the surveillance process, with the steps chosen to be epidemiologically meaningful for the system’s purpose (CDC 1988; CDC 2001; Hoinville 2013; Drewe 2015).
Median reporting delay: calculating the median number of days between a reference date, such as disease onset or diagnosis, and the date of report to the receiving agency (Jajosky 2004).
Benchmarking against the disease time course: expressing the measured interval as the percentage of cases reported within one or more incubation periods for the health event (Jajosky 2004; Buehler 2004).
Proportion reported within a target window: the share of reports or outbreak notifications submitted within a predefined schedule, such as 24 or 48 hours (WHO 2006; ECDC 2014).
Interim-milestone timeline: mapping fixed milestones along the surveillance chain to locate and compare the intervals that drive overall timeliness (Buehler 2004; Crawley 2021).
Alert lead-time comparison: comparing the time at which a statistical alert is generated against detection by an established surveillance component (Buehler 2008; Groseclose 2013).
Normalized timeliness score: modelling the measured interval with an exponential decay function to obtain a score between 0 and 1 (Arinik 2023).
Trend analysis of median timeliness: applying Cox proportional hazards regression to assess changes in median timeliness over time (Crawley 2021).
Time-to-detection against a reference indicator: estimating the lead time between an environmental or surveillance signal and a clinical or gold-standard indicator (Amato 2023; Arinik 2023).
Qualitative key-informant assessment: interviewing system operators to judge whether the achieved intervals meet the surveillance purpose (Harper 2011; Groseclose 2010).

title: Methods
text:
PHES-EF is being developed using an established, internationally recognized consensus methodology. The study follows its published protocol and will be reported using the ACCORD guideline for consensus studies, with PRISMA-ScR for the scoping reviews and GRIPP2 for public involvement. This approach ensures:


Evidence-based content through two systematic scoping reviews
International consensus via a two-round e-Delphi survey and a consensus meeting
Diverse perspectives from content experts, knowledge users and engaged members of the public
Transparent development with open sharing of materials and progress on the Open Science Framework
Broad applicability across public health environmental surveillance systems, using wastewater-based surveillance as an example


The framework will be developed in five steps.





1





Agree on the scope of the study and develop the study protocol
Agree on terms of reference for executive group members

Completed



2





Conduct scoping reviews to extract candidate items for the e-Delphi survey (searches are being updated)
Review candidate items with the executive group for organization, completeness and redundancy

In progress



3





Recruit, screen and register international panellists (registration opens January 2027)
Run two online survey rounds in spring 2027

Upcoming



4





Hold a hybrid or virtual consensus meeting in September or October 2027
Reach expert consensus on the final list of items and agree on dissemination strategies

Upcoming



5





Post a preprint to OSF, then submit to an open-access peer-reviewed journal (late 2027), under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence
Engage researchers and knowledge users, and support adoption of the framework

Upcoming




A multinational and multidisciplinary executive group will oversee the development of the evaluation framework. The group will bring expertise from various fields, including public health, infectious disease, epidemiology, environmental and physical sciences, mathematical sciences, social sciences, communication, knowledge translation and exchange, knowledge users, and an engaged public.
The executive group will be responsible for providing feedback on the framework development process (e.g., framework organization, completeness, additions, redundancy), supporting and advising working groups in their area of expertise, connecting the study to other related projects, recruiting e-Delphi panellists, participating in the consensus meeting, disseminating the evaluation framework, advising and/or participating in post-publication activities, and promoting the adoption of the evaluation framework among their professional networks. Co-chairs will also be responsible for decision-making when the executive group cannot reach a consensus, leading executive group activities, and the overall framework development process.
For more information about the members of the study’s Executive Group, please visit the Team page.



We will systematically compile a list of e-Delphi candidate items through scoping reviews, content analysis and extraction, and executive group consultation.
You can view relevant scoping review registrations and publications on our Documents page.



A Delphi technique will be used to develop an internationally accepted evaluation framework for public health environmental surveillance. The Delphi method is an iterative multi-round approach that uses a series of sequential surveys, interspersed by controlled feedback, to elicit consensus among a group of individuals while maintaining anonymity (1,2). An e-Delphi method will be used to overcome geographic barriers and allow us to engage panellists internationally across various time zones.

title: About
text:
PHES-EF (Public Health Environmental Surveillance Evaluation Framework) is an international consensus study to develop a framework for evaluating public health environmental surveillance systems, using wastewater-based surveillance as an example.

Evaluation framework definition: An evaluation framework is a structured system designed to systematically assess the effectiveness and impact of a program (1,2). It typically outlines key components - such as domains, concepts, and indicators or measures - that should be included in an evaluation. It also provides a logical organization of these components, explains the process by which they were identified and prioritized, and may offer guidance on how to measure them. By offering a comprehensive and transparent basis for evaluation, such frameworks support informed decision-making and help identify areas for improvement in public health programs.





Theme
A high-level grouping of related concepts that define broad areas of public health evaluation.
Example: Surveillance effectiveness


Domain
A major area of focus within a theme.
Example: Data quality


Subdomain
A specific aspect or perspective within a domain.
Example: Ascertainment performance


Attribute
A measurable property or characteristic.
Example: Sensitivity




Public health environmental surveillance has evolved, especially during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, with wastewater surveillance being a prominent example. As surveillance methods diversify and expand, there is a need to evaluate these systems to improve the evidence of wastewater surveillance effectiveness, return-on-investment, accountability, transparency, sustainability and trust.
There is also a need for such an evaluation framework as the recent adoption of wastewater-based monitoring has resulted in a lack of standard analytic techniques, with preferred methods for reporting testing data still remaining unclear (3). PHES-EF aims to address this issue as well, as the framework is intended to be adopted by researchers to determine surveillance system performance and create analogous results for comparison within the field.



The Delphi method is an iterative multi-round approach that uses a series of sequential surveys, interspersed by controlled feedback, to elicit consensus among a group of individuals while maintaining anonymity (4,5). An electronic Delphi (e-Delphi) method will be used to overcome geographic barriers and allow us to engage panellists internationally across various time zones. Delphi surveys relating to health sciences have typically been conducted over a period of 2-3 rounds (6–8). Therefore, a two-round e-Delphi survey paired with a subsequent consensus meeting will be conducted to balance feasibility with rigour. Each round will be open for about five weeks to allow panellists sufficient time to participate in the survey, while balancing study timeline constraints (9). Each round takes about an hour to complete. The consensus meeting will be held in a hybrid or virtual format.

For licensing details, please refer to the license section of this page.





“Equity is defined as the removal of systemic barriers and biases enabling all individuals to have equal opportunity to access and benefit from the program” (10). To achieve this, members of the research team are committed to developing a strong understanding of the systemic barriers faced by individuals from underrepresented groups.
“Diversity is defined as differences in race, colour, place of origin, religion, immigrant and newcomer status, ethnic origin, ability, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and age” (10). Panellists will be asked to provide characteristic information (e.g., country of residence, gender, primary discipline) to assess and help ensure (through more targeted recruitment) a large diversity in perspectives.
“Inclusion is defined as the practice of ensuring that all individuals are valued and respected for their contributions and are equally supported” (10). To help ensure that all research team members are integrated and supported, we will have a code of conduct statement in the executive group Terms of Reference.
All study working group members will complete EDI-related Canadian Institutes for Health Research (CIHR) Training, and the First Nations principles of Ownership, Control, Access and Possession (OCAP©) training for the research (11). The executive group will receive an overview of EDI and OCAP and will be encouraged and supported to complete such training. Furthermore, staff trained in EDI and OCAP principles will review the framework from an EDI perspective to ensure appropriate language.





To ensure accurate and transparent reporting of knowledge users and public involvement throughout the study, we will refer to the Guidance for Reporting Involvement of Patients and the Public (GRIPP2) checklist (12). We will document the methods used to engage knowledge users, report the impacts and outcomes of their engagement, and report on lessons learned from the experience.

We will recruit a multinational, multidisciplinary panel of wastewater-based surveillance experts, knowledge users, and engaged members of the public to complete the e-Delphi survey. Panellists will be selected to capture the multiple perspectives of those that influence the design, implementation, evaluation, use, and reporting of wastewater surveillance activities, including the following subdisciplines groups: public health, infectious disease, epidemiology; environmental and physical sciences; mathematical sciences; social sciences; and communication, knowledge translation and exchange.
We will aim to recruit at least 50 panellists, preferably with at least 8 to 10 people per discipline subgroup. Registration opens about four weeks before Round 1, and recruitment continues during both rounds. Panellists complete a short screening questionnaire and then receive an anonymous link to the survey. The study working group will monitor the distribution of registered panellists based on their demographic information and will try to distribute appropriately across discipline subgroups and other demographic markers.






Content experts

Expertise subgroups:

Public health, infectious disease, epidemiology
Environmental and physical sciences
Mathematical sciences
Social sciences
Communication, knowledge translation and exchange



An adult1
Proficient in English
Has a graduate degree in one of the listed specializations2, or ≥ 3 years of professional experience, or ≥ 2 peer-reviewed publications relating to wastewater surveillance

Definitions: Professional experience: paid employment or professional practice in a listed specialization (current or former). Graduate or professional degree: Master or PhD in a listed discipline/specialization.





We will conduct a two-round e-Delphi survey to generate consensus on evaluation criteria (Figure 2). Summaries of Round 1 will be compiled for the subsequent round. Custom survey pathways will be generated for each stakeholder group (i.e., panellists from different stakeholder groups will be shown a different collection of candidate items). Within each custom stakeholder survey pathway, panellists will also have the option to skip items or self-declare that they are not qualified to assess certain candidate items.


Panellists will rate each candidate item shown to them in their expertise pathway on whether it should be included in an evaluation framework, using a 7-point Likert scale. Candidate items are generated from scoping review results and consultation with the study executive group. Free-text boxes will be included for panellists to provide feedback or suggest new candidate items for the next round. Items that reach consensus in Round 1 will not be re-rated in Round 2.
Round 1 will be open for about five weeks, take about an hour to complete, and include two email reminders.



Regardless of whether they participated in the previous round, panellists will be invited to participate in Round 2 of the e-Delphi survey. All panellists will be invited to rate new items and re-rate previous items that did not reach consensus. Items in Round 2 will be rated across four rating properties (see below). When re-rating their level of agreement, panellists will be presented with their previous round scores alongside the aggregate group results. Anonymous feedback from Round 1 will also be compiled and presented during Round 2. Any newly suggested items during Round 2 will be deliberated on during the consensus meeting.



In Round 2, candidate items will be assessed on the following four rating properties: (1) relevance and practical utility; (2) scientific rigor, validity and reliability; (3) feasibility, adaptability and resource implications; and (4) equity, inclusiveness, and mitigation of bias.
A 7-point Likert scale (1 = highly irrelevant to 7 = highly relevant) will be used to rate each property. A summary score for each candidate item will be created by calculating the median of the four property ratings. In Round 1, the single inclusion rating is used directly. Panellist ratings will then be categorised as excluded item (irrelevant: 1–2), further discussion (equivocal: 3–5), or core item (relevant: 6–7). Consensus for each item is defined as ≥ 70% of the panellist votes falling within the same category (1–2, 3–5, or 6–7).
The approach to use a 7-point fully-labeled Likert scale – a higher number of categories compared to many studies – is informed by the consideration that panellists are professionals and engaged members of the public with good cognitive skills; therefore, more categories and labels will be more discriminating and reproducible (3–6). The ≥ 70% consensus cut-off – a lower cut-off compared to many studies – is informed by the rapidly evolving nature of environmental surveillance for public health and the wide range of disciplines invited to the panel; therefore, a high level of agreement may not occur (3–6).

text:
We will recruit a multinational, multidisciplinary panel of wastewater-based surveillance experts, knowledge users, and engaged members of the public to complete the e-Delphi survey. Panellists will be selected to capture the multiple perspectives of those that influence the design, implementation, evaluation, use, and reporting of wastewater surveillance activities, including the following subdisciplines groups: public health, infectious disease, epidemiology; environmental and physical sciences; mathematical sciences; social sciences; and communication, knowledge translation and exchange.
We will aim to recruit at least 50 panellists, preferably with at least 8 to 10 people per discipline subgroup. Registration opens about four weeks before Round 1, and recruitment continues during both rounds. Panellists complete a short screening questionnaire and then receive an anonymous link to the survey. The study working group will monitor the distribution of registered panellists based on their demographic information and will try to distribute appropriately across discipline subgroups and other demographic markers.

Executive group
The executive group oversees and supports the development of PHES-EF. Co-chaired by Doug Manuel and David Buckeridge, it brings together members from five World Bank regions and all five of the study’s discipline subgroups: public health, infectious disease and epidemiology; environmental and physical sciences; mathematical sciences; social sciences; and communication, knowledge translation and exchange.
Members contribute by:


reviewing the candidate evaluation items for their organization, completeness, gaps and redundancy
advising the study working group in their areas of expertise
connecting the study with related projects and networks
helping identify e-Delphi panellists and promoting the survey among their professional contacts
taking part in the consensus meeting to agree on the final framework
guiding dissemination and promoting adoption of the framework among actors and end-users

Doug Manuel is a Distinguished Professor at the University of Ottawa in the Departments of Family Medicine and School of Epidemiology and Public Health. He is a Senior Scientist at The Ottawa Hospital Research Institute, and a Senior Investigator at the Bruyère Health Research Institute. Dr. Manuel holds an M.D. from Dalhousie University, and M.Sc. in Epidemiology and Royal College Speciality in Public Health from the University of Toronto.


He leads the development of the Public Health Environmental Surveillance Open Data Model (PHES ODM) which is used worldwide for wastewater surveillance. He consults for the World Bank for the development of wastewater surveillance in low- and middle-income countries. He formerly led the Coronavirus Variants Rapid Response Network (CoVaRR-Net) Wastewater Research Group.

Mary is the lead researcher for CIEDAR’s #BeadAndThrive social media engagement. They joined CIEDAR after working as a research and data analytics officer for the Department of Canadian Heritage, where their focus on equity and inclusion helped inform the governance of Canada’s diverse populations (i.e., 2SLGBTQ+, Persons Living with Disabilities, and Indigenous Peoples). Mary is also a PhD student in the Department of Sociology at the University of British Columbia. Their research focuses on assortative mating patterns among gender diverse (i.e., transgender and non-binary) Canadians and how these patterns reproduce socio-economic inequalities.
